extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and instructors of American government and public administration; general readers interested in U.S. federal administrative structure
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-level survey of the powers, duties, organization, and practices of the U.S. national administration (executive departments, the Cabinet, and the civil service). Explains statutory and customary rules that govern departmental officers and administrative procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential budget-review authority (1909 law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of 1909 authorizes the President to review the estimated expenditures and revenues and make specific recommendations to Congress as to the best methods to be employed in securing a satisfactory balance in the budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law 'shifts to the President a large burden of responsibility which has hitherto rested on Congress' and 'undoubtedly will give an additional weight to executive influence in legislative matters.' The passage highlights the practical effect of transferring budgetary initiative to the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of non-members to speak in Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The houses, either separately or jointly, may admit persons who are not members and authorize them to speak on any matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically cabinet officers and executive officials have appeared before the Senate and House to explain measures and read messages; the Constitution would prevent heads of departments from being members at the same time, but does not prevent their being admitted to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of Treasury reporting duty (Act of 1789)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act organizing the Treasury provided that the Secretary 'shall, from time to time, digest and prepare plans for the improvement and management of the revenue and for the support of public credit ... shall make reports and give information to either branch of the legislature, in person or in writing as may be required, respecting all matters referred to him by the Senate or House of Representatives or which shall appertain to his office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory provision exemplifies an early, explicit duty of departmental heads to inform the legislature, whether in person or in writing, on matters pertaining to their offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting cabinet officers to appear before Congress (1881 Senate committee position)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Senate committee in 1881 reported in favor of giving heads of departments the right to appear in Congress, arguing such practice was not a violation of separation of powers and would make information given to Congress more pertinent and conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee urged that allowing appearances 'would put the members of the legislature on the alert' and suggested appointment of under-secretaries to handle routine business so chiefs could address larger policy duties. The recommendation was, however, not adopted widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on subordinate communications to Congress (Taft 1909 order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order (Nov 26, 1909): 'no bureau, office, or division chief, or subordinate in any department of the Government... shall apply to either House of Congress, or to any committee... or to any Member of Congress for legislation or for appropriations or for congressional action of any kind, except with the consent and knowledge of the head of the department; nor shall any such person respond to any request for information... except through, or as authorized by, the head of his department.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended 'to cut off the subterranean connection between the subordinates in the executive departments and Congress' and to centralize official congressional communications through departmental heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on Presidential control over statutory departmental duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the President appoints and may remove heads of departments, 'the President cannot alter or diminish any of the duties laid down by Congress, and cannot prevent Congress from imposing or taking away duties' prescribed by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation from J. Sherman: departmental officers are intrusted with powers by Constitution and laws; the President has no more right to control the powers conferred by law upon them than they have to control him. In practice, removal power may be used by strong Presidents to direct subordinates, producing variations from the strict legal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental appointing and removal powers subject to civil service rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A large appointing power to minor offices is conferred by law upon the departmental head, but this is now exercised under civil service rules which restrict his choice in all except the important subordinate positions to candidates who have qualified by examination; the power of removal generally accompanies the power of appointment, although there are some important exceptions by law and by executive order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil service laws and classification limit patronage; appointments to classified posts are made on merit/examination, reducing the head's discretion except for key positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory authority of departmental heads
rubrics_metrics.description: By act of Congress, a departmental head may 'prescribe regulations, not inconsistent with law, for the government of his department, the conduct of its officers and clerks, the distribution and performance of its business, and the custody, use, and preservation of the records, papers, and property appertaining to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory grant gives departmental chiefs a range of freedom to issue internal departmental orders, subject to the limitation they not conflict with law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual departmental report requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every departmental chief must prepare annually a report of his department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes such reports are largely formal compilations and often have little direct influence on legislation, though they are an established mechanism of informing Congress and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customary, indirect methods for department influence on legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Cabinet officers cannot be members of Congress, 'custom has decreed' that they bring influence to bear by circuitous ways: appearing before committees, transmitting completed drafts of bills, and establishing relations with committee chairmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes accepted, informal channels through which the executive shapes legislation without direct floor membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of accessibility and attention to outside parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Heads of departments are subjected to constant interruptions from outside parties; they must give heed to innumerable trifles and requests from people of importance, taking them up with care required by their position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates democratic expectation for departmental accessibility and the practical burden on high officials to accommodate visitors, senators, congressmen, and political leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of certain administrative determinations (limited judicial review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes and practice give departmental officers final authority in many administrative matters (e.g., immigration decisions by immigration officers are final unless reversed on appeal to the Secretary of Labor; customs appraisements and certain Postmaster-General determinations are generally not reviewed by courts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have recognized that review of routine administrative determinations would cause confusion and impair government functions; nevertheless, judicial review remains available where it can be shown the official exceeded jurisdiction or violated the law. The book cites cases and policy rationales balancing executive necessity and individual rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postmaster-General's fraud-order authority (non-reviewable facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Postmaster-General may issue fraud orders denying the use of the mails to persons and concerns who in his opinion are engaged in fraudulent transactions; those affected have no right to appeal to the courts for a review of the facts on which he bases his decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by judicial reasoning that requiring court review of such day-to-day administrative judgments would practically arrest executive functions; nevertheless, individuals retain 'an ultimate recourse to the judiciary' on legal questions or jurisdictional excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet's informal legal status and secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cabinet, as a collective body, has no legal existence or power; Cabinet meetings are usually secret, no record is kept of transactions, and the Cabinet is not subjected as such to congressional control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although informal, the Cabinet functions as the President's confidential advisers and council; meetings are used primarily to maintain departmental cooperation and work out matters of general policy rather than to make formal votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and composition of executive departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Each department is organized into a secretary, assistants, chief clerks, and multiple bureaus/divisions (the text lists State, Treasury, War, Justice, Post-Office, Navy, Interior, Agriculture, Commerce, Labor and their subdivisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The catalogue gives definiteness to the administrative framework and indicates the multiplicity of offices and specialized bureaus; it also mentions salary information and that principal functions are discussed elsewhere in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil Service Commission composition and duty (Civil Service Act of 1883)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act provides for a Civil Service Commission composed of three persons, no more than two of whom shall be adherents of the same party, appointed by the President and Senate, and charged with the duty of aiding the President ... in preparing suitable rules for competitive examinations designed to test the fitness of applicants for offices in the public service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission aids the President generally in execution of the Act, prepares examinations, and helps organize the classified service; it is the statutory mechanism for implementing the merit system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of positions and extension of the merit system
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act ordered certain classifications (Secretaries to make classifications) and left extension of the principle largely to the discretion of the President and future acts of Congress; since then executive orders and statutes have steadily increased the number of classified positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include President Roosevelt's extensions (rural free delivery, census office classification, forestry service, immigration special agents), illustrating how the merit system was expanded over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for civil service examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act requires that such examinations shall be practical in their character, and, so far as may be, relate to those matters which will fairly test the relative capacity and fitness of persons examined to discharge the duties of that branch of the government service to which they seek to be admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In preparing examination papers the Commission commonly cooperates with departments; technical positions often have technical questions prepared by the department concerned to adequately test fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convenience requirement for boards of examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act orders that boards of examiners shall be erected at such points as to make it reasonably convenient and inexpensive for applicants to attend examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a chief examiner at Washington and several hundred local boards scattered among states and territories to supervise local civil service examinations; logistical placement is required to facilitate applicants' attendance.
